It was mentioned at the Physlib Cafe yesterday that a good project to start would be the scattering of particles. Even though we're not in a position to connect this directly to, for example, the standard model, it would still be good to have a nice API around this designed. The idea is to be able to describe the sort of scattering diagrams as written below, along with the corresponding selection rules.

π−+p→π0+n\pi^- + p \to \pi^0 + n % charge exchangeπ−+p→π0+n

π−+p→K0+Λ0\pi^- + p \to K^0 + \Lambda^0 % associated production of strangenessπ−+p→K0+Λ0

p+p→p+pp + p \to p + p % elastic pp, ISR/LHC total cross sectionp+p→p+p

pˉ+p→π++π−\bar{p} + p \to \pi^+ + \pi^- % annihilationpˉ​+p→π++π−
Anyone who wants to help contribute to this project or has ideas of how we can best do it, I think we would be very glad to know!
Sounds fun! So it would be some feynman diagram computation machinery?

I think Feynman diagrams themselves would not be within the scope of this project, as they would need to connect to e.g. Wicks theorem, which is a longer term goal. But the selection rules which determine the ingoing and outgoing states of a Feynman diagram would be.

As discussed as well, we could approach PDG for some input on the mass and JP(C) quantum numbers for mesons (baryons) without replicating this as tables... Initially we could likely limit this scope to the ground state SU(3) flavor multiplets definitionally without deriving them (which will require some more Lie algebra).

So, first API target could be something like a particle, which has a mass, J, P, C, and later S, B? I'd love to see the structure @Tyler Josephson ⚛️ uses for elements/molecules.
OK gotcha, scattering diagrams meant these reaction channels, so its about the representation theory only

PDG provides sqlite databases (https://pdg.lbl.gov/2026/api/index.html), and Lean has sqlite bindings (https://github.com/leanprover/leansqlite). Is that a reasonable approach for this? Not sure how this would work... (can lake pull external sqlite files to use during build?)

I suspect that reading in an sqlite database would certainly not be possible while remaining within the "standard axioms of Lean". Another approach might be to come up with some way to automatically exact that data from the sqlite database and tag it in the Lean code, so in the future it is easy to update.
If we go down the PdG route, it would also be good to associate decays and scatterings with their associated experimental data.

I don't know much about the this kind of scattering, but here's the high-level architecture I'm implementing in LeanCatalyst:

Traditional scientific computing software take input files describing simulation / analysis options and initial conditions / data. I'm generally used to these being some combination of a software-specific input file (usually acting as text file, though not usually the .txt extension) + some kind of data file (e.g. something very generic like .csv or .yaml or json, or something domain-specific, like how molecular coordinates can be specified as .pdb or .mol or .xyz).

My approach to LeanCatalyst has been to have an unverified external tool (a long, vibe-coded Python script) transcribe the software-specific input file into a .lean file of my custom design, which carries proofs of correctness. This way, I can start with a .yaml file compatible with Cantera (an incumbent python-based chemistry software), which can still be run by the legacy software for the purposes of testing and comparing. The .yaml is then converted into a .lean file (again, by an unverified Python script that simply reads the old format and prints the new format) that stores this information in Lean objects. The .lean input file all by itself represents a verified entity - not verifying that the numbers it imported are correct (can't really do that in Lean - at some point, you just need to trust the source of the data), but verifying whatever specifications you can think of that should be satisfied in the input file (because the input .lean has top-line imports for math or scientific information).

In the case of LeanCatalyst, I import the types and definitions around reactions, molecules, and stoichiometry at the top of input.lean. Then, we write down individual reactions as Lean defs, which are guaranteed to satisfy atom balances when they type check. These Lean defs are being written down by the unverified Python translator code. For what it's worth, running the .yaml through Cantera functions and my input.lean through LeanCatalyst gets bit-level agreement on what should be the same run - without that, I wouldn't trust much in terms of semantics.

So, I think this architecture could be brought into other workflows (like scattering theorems + experimental data). I'd recommend getting the theorems in place and the Lean code executing something that can be compared to existing software before trying to build an input file converter.

Here's the current version of those files:

rmg2lean.py
CH4O2Pt.yaml
CH4O2Pt.lean
